hook: "Games keep score, maps keep scale and apps keep your settings. All of them store a value under a name and calculate with it."
app:
  command: "node \"$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs\" \"$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground\" 8123"
  url: "http://127.0.0.1:8123/index.html"
  ready: Python code
  layout: full

explainClip:
  query: { code: "", speed: 8 }
  caption: "A variable is a name for a value"
  say: "A variable is a name for a value, like a labelled box."
  pacing: { keyDelayMs: 22 }
  clip:
    - caption:
        text: "sides = 5 stores 5 in a box called sides."
        say: "sides equals 5 stores five in a box called sides."
    - type: { into: "Python code", text: "from turtle import *\n\nsides = 5\n", append: true }
    - caption:
        text: "angle = 360 / sides works out the turn for you."
        say: "angle equals 360 divided by sides works out the turn for you."

    - type: { into: "Python code", text: "8", after: "sides = " }

In the last lesson the numbers were typed straight into each command. Here you give a number a **name**, so you can change it in one place and let the program work out the rest.

## Predict

```step
stage: predict
code: variables.py#polygon
check:
  type: predict
  q: "How many sides will the shape have?"
  kind: number
  actual: "Five sides. angle = 360 / 5 = 72, so the turtle turns 72 degrees at each corner and the shape closes."
```

`angle = 360 / sides` stores the result of a calculation. What will the turtle draw? How many sides, and why does `right(angle)` turn by that amount?

## Run

```step
stage: run
code: variables.py#polygon
try: { starter: "variables.py#polygon", height: 420 }
```

Run it and compare it with your prediction.

Here is what each line does.

| Line | What it does | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `sides = 5` | Stores 5 under the name `sides` | Read `=` as "store": put 5 in a box called `sides` |
| `size = 80` | Stores 80 under the name `size` | Change it here and every `size` below changes |
| `angle = 360 / sides` | Works out the turn and stores it | A full turn is 360 degrees, split between the corners |
| `range(sides)` | Repeats `sides` times | The name stands in for 5 |
| `right(angle)` | Turns by whatever `angle` holds | 72 here, but you never typed 72 |

Change `sides` and the turn updates by itself.

## Investigate

```step
stage: investigate
code: variables.py#print
insight: "A variable is a named value: you can follow how it is used, find where it goes wrong, and change it in one place."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: number
      q: "If sides = 6, what is angle?"
      answer: 60
      explain: "360 / 6 = 60, so the turtle turns 60 degrees at each corner."
  - check:
      type: bug
      code: variables.py#bug
      text: "This program should draw a 5-sided shape, but it does not close. Click the wrong line."
      answer: 5
      fault: logic
      misconception: angle-from-sides
      explain: "angle = 360 * sides is too big. To split one full turn between the corners it should be 360 / sides."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "The program stores size = 50 and draws a line. Later it stores size = 100 and draws another line. How long was the first line?"
      options: ["50", "100", "150", "Storing size twice is an error"]
      answer: 0
      fault: logic
      misconception: variable-copies-later
      explain: "A line uses the value size holds at that moment. Storing a new value changes the lines drawn after it, not the ones already drawn."
  - check:
      type: bug
      code: variables.py#bug-indent
      text: "This should draw a hexagon, but the turtle draws one long line and turns once at the end. Click the wrong line."
      answer: 9
      fault: logic
      misconception: loop-body-indent
      explain: "right(angle) is not indented, so it is not part of the loop. Indent it under the for line so both lines repeat."
```

`print(angle)` shows a value under the drawing. Copy it whenever you want to see what a name holds; the console lessons explain how it works. Change `sides` and watch what `angle` becomes, then work through the checks.

### Calculate the angle

Work out `angle` yourself before you check.

### Spot the bug

Something small in here stops the shape from closing.

### A name keeps its value

A name holds one value at a time. Lines that ran earlier keep what they used.

```python
size = 50
forward(size)
size = 100
forward(size)
```

### Spot the bug in the loop

You have met this one before, now with names in it.

## Modify

```step
stage: modify
insight: "Changing the program through a variable is safer than changing many numbers: one edit, whole shape updated."
try: { starter: "variables.py#modify", height: 420 }
hint: "You should only need to change one number. Which variable controls the number of sides?"
check: { type: reflect, text: "I changed one variable and the whole shape updated." }
```

Change one number at the top to draw a hexagon, then a 12-sided shape. Run it each time.

## Make

```step
stage: make
try: { starter: "variables.py#make", height: 420 }
hint:
  - "Put three names at the top: sides, size and colour. Then use each name below."
  - "A colour is text, so it goes in quotes: colour = \"purple\". Use it with pencolor(colour)."
check: { type: code, text: "Use a variable for the pen colour and draw a shape with a loop.", rules: { uses: [pencolor], loops: 1 } }
unlocks: [named-turn]
smaller:
  check:
    type: question
    q: "You wrote colour = \"purple\" at the top. Which line uses it to colour the pen?"
    options: ["pencolor(colour)", "pencolor(\"colour\")", "colour(pencolor)", "pencolor = colour"]
    answer: 0
    feedback:
      - null
      - "In quotes it is the word colour, which is not a colour. Without quotes it is whatever the name holds."
      - "pencolor is the thing that does the work, so it comes first, with the colour in brackets."
      - "The brackets hand the colour to pencolor. An equals sign would be a variable of its own."
    explain: "No quotes means \"use what colour holds\", so pencolor(colour) paints with purple."
```

Make your own shape generator. Put three names at the top (`sides`, `size` and `colour`) and use all three below. Then change each one and watch the shape change.

## Resize a room plan

```step
stage: modify
try: { starter: "variables.py#plan", height: 420 }
```

Plans and maps store a **scale**: how many pixels are one metre. This program draws a 6 m by 4 m room. Change the room to 8 m by 5 m, then change `scale` and notice the whole plan resizes. Then add a second room beside it.

```teacher
summary: Students give numbers names (variables) and let the program calculate
  the turn, so one change at the top updates the whole shape.
time: 40
timing: Predict and Run 10 min · Investigate 12 min · Modify 6 min · Make 8 min
  · Room plan 4 min
goals:
  - I can store a value in a variable and use its name instead of the number.
  - I can work out a value with a calculation, such as angle = 360 / sides.
  - I can change a whole drawing by changing one variable.
before: >
  Run the first program, then make the shape generator from the Make step.
  Notice how little you change to get a different shape: that is the point of
  the lesson.
running:
  - "Predict: ask how many sides the shape will have and why the turtle turns 72
    degrees. The answer is in the line angle = 360 / sides."
  - Read = aloud as 'store'. sides = 5 means 'store 5 in sides', not 'sides
    equals 5'. This one habit prevents most confusion later.
  - "Investigate: students work the angle for 6 sides, find the
    multiply-for-divide bug, decide what a later store does to a line already
    drawn (it does nothing to it), and find the unindented turn in a loop they
    met last lesson."
  - "Modify: students should only ever change the top numbers. If someone edits
    inside the loop, ask them to find the one variable that does the job."
  - "Make: three names and a loop. Let students choose their own values; the
    check only needs a variable-coloured pen and a loop."
stuck:
  - see: The shape does not close, or the turtle spins in place.
    ask: What is stored in angle when sides is 5? Work it out on paper.
    fix: angle must be 360 / sides (divide, not multiply).
  - see: A NameError says a name is not defined.
    ask: Is the name spelt exactly the same everywhere, including capitals?
    fix: Variable names must match exactly. Size and size are different names.
  - see: A student changes a variable after the loop and expects the shape to
      change.
    ask: Which lines already ran before you changed it?
    fix: Lines use the value a name holds when they run. Put the change above the
      loop.
stretch: Change sides to 3, 4, 5 and up to 20, and record which values still
  look like the shape and which look like a circle.
support: Give students a table with two columns (sides, angle) and ask them to
  fill in angle for 3, 4, 5 and 6 before running anything.
leads: "Next lesson uses the loop counter, so a value can change each pass
  without being typed. After that, a value that grows. Scores, game settings and
  the scale on maps and plans all use variables. Class ideas: a spiral gallery;
  scale drawings of the classroom."
exit:
  q: A program has sides = 8 and angle = 360 / sides. How far does the turtle turn
    at each corner?
  a: 45 degrees (360 divided by 8).
explain: >
  A **variable** is a name for a value. `sides = 5` means "store 5 in a box
  called sides". After that, every time the program sees `sides`, it uses 5.


  Variables can hold the result of a calculation: `angle = 360 / sides` works
  out the turn for you. Change `sides` and the turn updates by itself.


  A line uses the value a name holds at the moment it runs. Storing a new value
  changes the lines that come after it, not the ones already run.
solutions:
  step-4: variables.py#sol-sides
  step-5: variables.py#sol-colour
  step-6: variables.py#sol-plan
struggle: Seeing that a name holds a value the program can reuse. Ask them to
  say, for each line, which stored value it uses.
class:
  activities:
    - at: start
      kind: info
      title: By the end of this lesson
      do: >
        Here is the finished program running. By the end of the lesson you will
        write one like it.
      notes: Run the finished example on the projector before anything else.
    - at: investigate
      title: Be the computer
      minutes: 5
      do: >
        Students hold cards for sides, size and colour. Change one card; the
        class says which drawing changes.
      notes: Make the idea physical before it goes back to the screen.
    - at: end
      title: Change one number
      minutes: 3
      do: >
        Swap screens with the next pair. Change one number in their generator
        and say what shape it will draw before you run it.
```
